summary: Defines RMON-2 MIB extensions for monitoring Differentiated Services Codepoint usage. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This lets a network tool count how many packets were marked with each priority label.

questions: how to monitor dscp usage with rmon
what is counter aggregation in dsmon
subtitle: An SNMP MIB that lets RMON probes count network traffic per Differentiated Services codepoint.

tldr.problem: Each Differentiated Services codepoint (DSCP) can get different treatment from forwarding devices, but there was no standard way to monitor how much traffic uses each codepoint.
tldr.mechanism: The DSMON MIB extends RMON-2 probes with tables that count packets and octets per DSCP, per protocol, per host and per host pair, with a configurable way to aggregate the 64 codepoint counters into groups.
tldr.outcome: A management station can poll these counters to see DSCP throughput and tune its QoS policy, without the probe having to look at a forwarding device's internal statistics.

today: RFC 3287 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What DSMON Monitors
sections.content:
RFC 3287 defines a piece of the Management Information Base (MIB) for monitoring Differentiated Services (DS) codepoint usage in packets that carry a DS field. It builds on the RMON-2 monitoring framework from RFC 2021. The DS field is the redefined Type of Service octet of the IP header (RFC 2474); its 6-bit codepoint (DSCP) gives 64 possible packet treatments, which affect which packets are dropped or delayed during congestion.

By polling DSCP counters, a network management station (NMS) can work out throughput for traffic per DSCP and then tune DSCP allocations to match the network's QoS policies. The counters are collected by RMON probes, which are separate software or hardware components. The RFC stresses that DSMON probes only collect and aggregate statistics from the content of monitored packets, and do not monitor any internal statistics of a DS forwarding device.

The module is written in SMIv2 and is a product of the RMONMIB working group, not the DIFFSERV group. Other metrics such as delay and jitter are out of scope.
sections.eli5: Some packets get VIP treatment and others wait in line. This MIB lets a watcher count how much traffic gets each kind of treatment.

sections.title: Reuse of RMON Concepts
sections.content:
DSMON is meant to be implemented in RMON probes that support RMON-2. Those probes may be stand-alone devices or co-located with other equipment such as Ethernet switches and repeaters. DSMON is independent of other RMON data tables, but borrows several ideas on purpose, so developers get 'MIB re-use'.

  • Protocol directory: the protocolDirLocalIndex object identifies protocol encapsulations in the tables that classify by protocol.
  • TimeFilter: lets an NMS retrieve only rows created or modified since its last poll, which keeps polling load down on large tables.
  • Zero-based counters: counters start at zero when management action creates them, using ZeroBasedCounter32 and ZeroBasedCounter64.
  • High capacity counters: where a 64-bit counter exists, a 32-bit version and a 32-bit overflow counter are also provided, for SNMPv1 coexistence.
  • TopN reports: the same reporting structure as RMON-2, to reduce polling overhead.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new counting machine, this MIB reuses parts of an existing one, like building a new toy from familiar blocks.

sections.title: Counter Aggregation
sections.content:
Keeping 64 separate counters for every collection can be wasteful, so DSMON lets the agent combine DSCP counters. A counter aggregation group is a set of counters combined into one. A counter aggregation profile is a complete set of 64 mappings, one per DSCP value 0 to 63. The RFC gives several reasons to aggregate: fewer counters in the agent, limited hardware counters, less polling for the application, unused codepoints, and codepoints that get the same packet treatment anyway.

Profiles are configured globally so that many collections and data sources can share them. Three tables do the work. The read-create dsmonAggControlTable has one entry per profile. The dsmonAggProfileTable has 64 rows per profile, indexed 0 to 63, each mapping one DSCP to a group; the agent SHOULD initially assign group zero. The dsmonAggGroupTable holds optional descriptive labels for groups.

The scalar dsmonMaxAggGroups reports the most groups allowed in a profile and SHOULD equal 64, though an agent MAY limit it. The scalar dsmonAggControlLocked is a switch for write access to the control tables. While it is false, all active DSMON collection data is deleted and collection is suspended, because changing the mappings could change what the collections mean.
sections.eli5: You can sort 64 colors of wristbands into a few buckets, like putting all the reds in one box. Then you only have to count the boxes.

sections.title: The MIB Groups
sections.content:
The module has six groups of objects, under the RMON branch as { rmon 26 }:

  • dsmonAggControl: configures counter aggregation groups.
  • dsmonStatsObjects: packet and octet distribution per aggregation group for a data source. This is the coarsest view, where analysis would start.
  • dsmonPdistObjects: the same per application protocol. It is hard-wired to application-layer (terminal) protocols and adds a maximum-entries parameter, insert and delete counters and LRU garbage collection.
  • dsmonHostObjects: per host, in and out. The protocol index MUST identify a network protocol that carries a DS field (such as IPv4 or IPv6). A configurable number of monitored address bits lets the agent zero the rightmost address bits to merge hosts into prefixes.
  • dsmonMatrixObjects: per host pair, source to destination.
  • dsmonCapsObjects: a single read-only dsmonCapabilities bit string that says which groups the agent supports.

The protocol, host and matrix groups each have a pair of TopN tables for periodic reports of the most-used combinations. The indexing follows the matching RMON-2 tables, with an added index for the aggregation group.
sections.eli5: There are different counting sheets. One counts per wristband color, one per app, one per computer, and one per pair of computers talking.

sections.title: Configuring Profiles Step by Step
sections.content:
Section 5 gives a seven-step example of how a management station could set up counter aggregation profiles. The RFC says clearly that it defines no standard, an agent need not support it, and the SET notation is only conceptual and not an actual SNMP Set PDU.

The steps are: unlock the configuration by setting dsmonAggControlLocked to false; check the maximum number of groups; check whether the profiles already exist; create the control entries; create the group descriptions; create the profile mappings; and lock the configuration again. The three example profiles are one DSCP per group, a collection of DIFFSERV PHBs, and a smaller aggregated set of PHBs.
sections.eli5: It is a checklist: open the settings, check what is already there, add your new buckets, then lock the settings again.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To implement this MIB, a probe must capture all packets on its local network, including those between third parties, and analyze them for addresses, protocol usage and conversation statistics. That data can be sensitive, so administrators may want to restrict SNMP access to the probe.

Objects with read-write or read-create access can also be sensitive, and SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations. SNMPv1 alone is not secure, even on a secure network. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, namely the User-based Security Model (RFC 2574) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575), and puts the burden on the user to configure access only for principals with legitimate rights.
sections.eli5: A counting machine that sees everyone's mail can learn a lot, so only trusted people should be allowed to ask it questions or change its settings.
